titulo: The Spanish clock is a gift
subtitulo: The hours the country actually eats at, the extra hour of table that comes free with the meal, and the two sentences that turn a seven o'clock wander into a half past nine booking
cena: Ten to seven, you are in a doorway with a menu in your hand, the dining room behind the waiter is empty, and he is holding the door open for you because tonight he needs your custom.
decisao: what time you sit down to eat — seven o'clock buys you the one kitchen in the street that lives off visitors, with the photographed menu and the bill that goes with it; half past nine buys you the room the neighbours are in, at the price they pay, plus an hour of table afterwards that nobody charges for

clique.desconto: You did not learn a new sentence tonight. You took the frame you already had and put tonight's hour into it.
clique.piso: You will book a Spanish table for half past nine and turn up hungry. Most visitors eat their whole fortnight at the one hour when only visitors are eating.

frasePiso: You will book a Spanish table for half past nine and turn up hungry. Most visitors eat their whole fortnight at the one hour when only visitors are eating.
permissao: You are allowed to eat at seven. It simply is not dinner: it is tapas at a counter, it costs less, and it is a proper plan that nobody thinks anything of. You are also allowed to take the whole hour after the plates go — the table is yours until you ask for the bill, and one more coffee is the only rent on it.
espelho: Standing up the moment the plates are cleared is the bit that reads as odd there. Leaving the second you have finished eating looks like the meal was a transaction you wanted over.

fichasCulturais.sinal: Twenty past seven, the lights are on, eight people at the counter with beers, and not one plate is coming out of the kitchen.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: They are shut, or they have looked at me and decided not to bother.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: The bar and the kitchen keep different hours under the same roof: the bar runs all day, the kitchen works two shifts and sleeps between them.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Ask at the door what time the kitchen opens, book a table for then, and go and have a drink somewhere with a view.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You get the kitchen at the hour it is actually cooking, and the two hours in between turn into the best part of the evening instead of a walk round the block.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not in a hotel dining room, an airport or a place on the main tourist street — those three cook straight through, and a full kitchen at seven is itself the sign of which kind of place you are standing in.

fichasCulturais.sinal: The plates went twenty minutes ago, nobody has come near your table, and the pair beside you have been sitting over one coffee since three.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: We have been forgotten, or they are waiting for us to take the hint and go.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: The table is let for the sitting and not for the plate. The hour after the food has a name, it is counted as part of the meal, and the bill only moves when you ask for it.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Stay where you are, order one more coffee, and let the conversation finish itself.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You get an hour of a good table for the price of a coffee, at the hour the room is at its best — and it is the hour in which strangers start talking to you.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not where the bill lands on the cloth without you asking. On a tourist strip that is a table being let twice in one evening, and there the hour is not on offer — you knew that from part fourteen.

steps.pt: Part nineteen. Warm-up: the punch. One syllable a word, and only one. Co-MI-da. La CE-na. So-bre-ME-sa.
Three of them, four of them, and the hit always in the same place. Hand on your leg, twice more.

steps.promptPt: Twenty past seven. The lights are on, eight people at the counter with beers, and not one plate in sight. One question at the door, before your coat comes off. Speak now.
steps.pt: the one to ask before you sit
👂 'Just drinks for now.' — what you will hear before eight, everywhere. It is not a closed door.
Ten to seven. You are in a doorway with a menu in your hand, and the dining room behind him is empty.
He is holding the door open for you. He is the one man in this street who needs your custom tonight.
Nobody has been rude to you and nothing has gone astray. You are four hours early, and that is all.
So here is the day the country is actually on. Coffee and toast before nine. A second coffee at eleven.
La comida, the big one, from two until half three. Something small at six. And la cena, from nine.
Kitchens wake up at eight, half eight. Last orders go in somewhere around half eleven. Typically, mind.
And none of that is a temperament. Spain sits over London's meridian and keeps Berlin's clock, since nineteen forty.
So the wall clock runs at least an hour ahead of the sun. Their nine is nearer your eight than it looks.

👂 on a card by the door: KITCHEN CLOSED — between shifts, not for the night.
The far end of the evening has an edge too, and it is the only part of this clock that catches people out.
Until what time do you serve?

steps.promptPt: Gone ten, a long walk behind you, and there is an end to the kitchen that nobody has mentioned yet. Find out where it is. Speak now.
steps.pt: where the evening ends
Half eleven, near enough. Which means ten o'clock is not late here. It is the middle of the evening.
So you book, and three in the afternoon is when to do it. The opener is the one you have had since part twelve.

steps.pt: And if half nine has gone, ask about the hour behind it. A good room fills twice on a Friday night.
Any table at ten? — the sitting almost nobody asks for, which is exactly why it is there.

Two more hours worth having. Around eleven the whole street stops for a second coffee and something small.

And getting up the moment the plates are cleared is the bit that reads as odd there. Nobody is waiting.
GUIRI ALERT. George here. My first Tuesday in Madrid I booked a table for half six, like a civilised man.
They took the booking. Of course they took it. I ate on my own, off a menu with photographs of the food.
Two streets over, at half ten, same money, room full. Nobody had misled me. I had simply arrived first.
And you do not have to eat at ten. Eat at seven and it is tapas at a counter, which is a proper plan.
What you skip is hunting a sit-down dinner at seven, because at seven only one kind of kitchen is cooking.
Count the places. The doorway. The pavement at three. The counter at eleven. The table at four. The hotel desk.

aprofundar.titulo: The clock, the meridian and the hour after the meal (optional reading)

secoes.corpo: Typical, not official — no Spanish institution publishes a national dinner time, so treat this as the shape of the day rather than a timetable pinned up at the border. Desayuno 07:30 to 09:00, and it is small: coffee and a toast with tomato and oil. A second coffee or a snack around 11:00, which is the one most visitors never notice and the one that fixes an early start. La comida, the main meal of the day, 14:00 to 15:30 or 16:00 — this is the big one, and it is where the menú del día lives. La merienda 17:00 to 18:30, coffee and something sweet. La cena from 21:00, with kitchens reopening around 20:00 to 20:30 and last orders somewhere near 23:30. Turning up between 18:00 and 19:00 gets you one of three answers: closed, open but drinks only, or open and empty — and open and empty at that hour is usually a house that survives on people who do not know the hours.

exemplos.pt: ah keh OH-rah AH-breh lah koh-THEE-nah — what time does the kitchen open? (the question that plans the evening)
AHS-tah keh OH-rah SEER-behn — until what time do you serve? (the other end of the same clock)

secoes.titulo: Why nine o'clock is not as late as it sounds
secoes.corpo: Mainland Spain sits over roughly the same line of longitude as London, and by the sun it belongs in the same hour as Britain. It does not run on that hour. In 1940 the clocks were moved forward to central European time and they were never moved back, which puts the whole country an hour ahead of its own daylight — two, in summer. A parliamentary commission recommended returning to the old zone in 2013 and nothing came of it. So when a table sits down to dinner at nine, the sun is roughly where a seven or eight o'clock sun would be at home, depending on the season, and lunch at half two is a one o'clock lunch by the light coming through the window. This is worth knowing for exactly one reason: it stops the schedule feeling like a national quirk you are being asked to accommodate, and turns it into arithmetic you can plan around. It is also why the light lasts so far into a summer evening.

exemplos.pt: lahs NWEH-beh deh lah NOH-cheh — nine at night, which by the sun is nearer eight

secoes.titulo: La sobremesa — the hour nobody bills you for
secoes.corpo: The plates go and nothing happens. No bill, no hovering, no one refilling your water pointedly. That gap has a name — la sobremesa, literally 'over the table' — and it is not the end of the meal, it is part of it: coffee, maybe something small and strong afterwards, and a conversation that is allowed to run. Two consequences for you. First, the bill genuinely will not come until you ask, which you already know from part fourteen; the waiter is not neglecting you, he is leaving you alone on purpose. Second, and this is the one that changes an afternoon: the table is yours for as long as you want it, and one more coffee is the whole rent. A Sunday lunch can still be at the table when the light changes. The counter-case is the one to watch for: if the bill lands on the cloth without you asking, that is a place letting the table twice, and you are being moved along politely. It happens on tourist strips and almost nowhere else.

exemplos.pt: OH-troh kah-FEH — another coffee, please (the rent on another hour of the table)
noh teh-NEH-mohs PREE-sah — 👂 we're in no hurry (what the next table says, and what the room assumes)

secoes.titulo: Booking, and telling the hour back
secoes.corpo: Restaurant booking runs on 'para las' plus the hour: para las nueve, para las diez. Half past is 'y media', quarter past 'y cuarto', quarter to 'menos cuarto' — so half past nine is 'las nueve y media' and quarter to ten is 'las diez menos cuarto'. Booking at half nine marks you instantly as somebody who did the reading, and in a busy place it is the sitting that goes first; ten o'clock is the one still going at eight in the evening. Two answers come straight back and you only ever have to recognise them: '¿para cuántas personas?' — for how many — and '¿a nombre de quién?' — under what name. Both are answered in two words. And for a phone booking, which you will occasionally have to make from a hotel desk, the same sentence works exactly as it does at the door: nothing about it changes on a telephone.

exemplos.es: Quería una mesa para las diez.
exemplos.pt: keh-REE-ah OO-nah MEH-sah PAH-rah lahs DYETH — I'd like a table for ten
ah NOM-breh deh kyen — 👂 under what name? (answer with your surname, spelled slowly)
